text_to_image.text: For sexual or erotic image requests, use direct literal wording instead of euphemism. State the exact participant count and identity ownership; visible anatomy and wardrobe state; pose, orientation, expression, gaze, and physical reaction; who touches or acts on whom; each visible contact point; body and prop placement; camera angle, shot scale, crop, focus, occlusion, lighting, and spatial relationship. Describe only what the camera can see, but make every requested visible anatomical interaction explicit. Keep limbs, anatomy, contact, shadows, reflections, and material response physically coherent. Do not replace requested action with generic intimacy, imply hidden or off-frame activity, add unrelated participants, or include process commentary.

image_to_image.title: Image to Image NSFW guidance
image_to_image.text: Treat each input image as bounded visual evidence. Preserve assigned identity, anatomy, wardrobe, pose, composition, lighting, environment, and object relationships unless the user explicitly requests a change. Describe the requested sexual or erotic edit directly, including the exact changed anatomy, wardrobe state, pose, action ownership, contact point, camera visibility, occlusion, expression, and resulting visible state. State what every reference controls and what incidental pose, background, framing, action, nudity, or participant it must not contribute. text_to_video.title: Text to Video NSFW guidance
text_to_video.text: For sexual or erotic video requests, write a concrete chronological audiovisual sequence rather than a mood summary. Establish participant count and identity, visible anatomy and wardrobe state, starting pose, environment, camera, lighting, and baseline sound. Give each timed beat one primary action that can fit naturally, reserve time for reactions and audible tails, and keep identity, anatomy, contact ownership, screen geography, props, lighting, and camera continuity stable. Do not rely on euphemism, hidden action, impossible motion, or unrelated participants.

Do not infer hidden anatomy, prior action, off-frame activity, audio, unrelated participants, or attributes the opening image does not show. first_last_frame_to_video.title: First-Last Frame to Video NSFW guidance

common_rules.title: Core Model Rules
common_rules.text: Write a literal, coherent Ideogram prompt. Preserve the user's subject, relationships, composition, medium, and every requested visible string exactly. Put the most important content first. Do not use weighting syntax, hidden flags, parameter notation, or unexplained tag soup.

common_guide.title: Profile Guide
common_guide.text:
## Literal natural-language prompting
Ideogram follows direct natural language. Start with the primary subject and defining action, then establish medium, environment, composition, viewpoint, lighting, color, mood, and finishing detail. Prefer concrete visible nouns and attributes over abstract quality claims. State spatial relationships explicitly: foreground/background, left/right/center, relative size, overlap, crop, and negative space.

## Composition and style
Describe framing and hierarchy in visual terms: shot scale, camera angle, focal point, depth, balance, symmetry or asymmetry, and the placement of supporting elements. Name the intended medium and aesthetic directly, such as editorial photograph, screen print, poster, watercolor, or 3D render. Keep style, materials, lighting, and color mutually coherent.

## Text and typography
Place every requested visible string in quotation marks with exact spelling, capitalization, and punctuation. Describe its location, hierarchy, font character, weight, color, alignment, and relationship to the image. Distinguish headline, subheading, label, and body copy. Do not invent text the user did not request.

profiles.label: SDXL
profiles.notes: SDXL uses text prompts with optional negative_prompt conditioning. It can use two text encoders in some pipelines, so prompts should separate concrete subject/composition from style/detail cues cleanly.

common_rules.title: Core Model Rules
common_rules.text: Write a high-signal SDXL prompt that preserves the user's intent. Prioritize the main subject and defining visual concepts, keep positive and negative concepts separate, and avoid contradictory style, lighting, anatomy, or composition instructions.

common_guide.title: Profile Guide
common_guide.text:
## Prompt anatomy
Lead with the main subject, identity-defining attributes, action or pose, and environment. Follow with composition, viewpoint, shot scale, lens or rendering perspective, lighting, color, materials, atmosphere, and medium. Use compact descriptive phrases where they improve concept recognition, but keep relationships grammatical enough to avoid attribute leakage between subjects.

## Emphasis and coherence
Repeat or foreground only genuinely important concepts; do not flood the prompt with near-synonyms. Keep camera terms compatible with the chosen medium and make lighting direction, time, weather, and shadow behavior agree. For multiple subjects, bind wardrobe, pose, props, and location to the correct subject. Describe visible text exactly and keep it short when possible.

## Negative guidance
When a separate negative output is requested, list only unwanted visual outcomes such as artifacts, malformed anatomy, duplicate elements, unintended text, watermark, blur, or style conflicts. Do not negate facts that are already required by the positive prompt.

Preserve requested writing verbatim, including language, spelling, punctuation, case, and line breaks when supplied. Describe the text's position and visual treatment. Do not translate, correct, or add words unless the user asks.

Add the minimum sufficient detail needed to remove ambiguity. Keep identities and counts stable, attribute clothing and props to the correct subject, and maintain plausible geometry, anatomy, lighting, and scene logic.

common_guide.title: Profile Guide
common_guide.text:
## Prompt expansion
Turn the brief into a long, coherent natural-language image description. Begin with the subject and intent, then develop action or pose, setting, composition, camera or viewpoint, lighting, color, materials, texture, atmosphere, and aesthetic. Preserve an explicitly requested medium rather than replacing it with a photograph or another style.

## Composition and physical description
Describe focal hierarchy, shot scale, crop, viewpoint, left/right/center placement, foreground and background, depth, negative space, and relationships among elements. Break complex poses into visible torso, head, hand, limb, balance, and contact states instead of relying only on a pose name. Keep anatomy and object interaction physically legible.

## Typography
Wrap requested visible words in quotation marks and preserve them exactly. Describe location, scale, font character, color, and integration with the image.

common_rules.title: Core Model Rules

common_guide.title: Profile Guide
common_guide.text:
## Prompt extension objective
Retain the user's original information, then add only cinematic details that make the requested video executable: subject appearance, environment, action, temporal development, camera movement, shot scale, lighting, atmosphere, and visual style. Use present-tense visual language and maintain a single coherent event.

## Motion and camera
Make movement the center of the video prompt. Describe the subject's trajectory, speed, direction, physical response, and interaction with the environment. common_guide.text:
## Complete scene description
Treat the prompt as the scene description, not a keyword list. State location, time, weather, subjects, wardrobe, props, initial pose, spatial layout, camera setup, lighting, visual style, and intended mood. Use enough detail for the duration: short clips need one focused action, while longer clips can carry more staged development.

## Temporal anatomy
Describe the established state before the first timed beat. Use timestamp ranges for meaningful changes, with consecutive, non-overlapping intervals scaled to the requested duration; if duration is absent, assume five seconds. After the last beat, state the final composition or held moment. Use beats to control action, reaction, camera, and sound—not to restate unchanged context.

## Motion and physical acting
Describe visible body mechanics: weight shift, posture, gaze, hands, contact, trajectory, pace, inertia, and environmental response. Keep actions achievable within the clip. Use specific verbs and avoid vague emotional labels when the emotion can be shown through face, breath, stance, or movement.

## Camera and capture style
Define shot scale, camera position, lens character or perspective, depth of field, movement, focus behavior, and capture aesthetic. Keep the camera plan consistent unless a change is intentional and timed. Prefer one continuous, intelligible camera idea over a stack of incompatible movements.

## Dialogue and audio
Write spoken lines verbatim and assign each line to the correct speaker at the moment it is heard. Integrate ambient sound, foley, impacts, vocal non-speech, and music into the timeline. Describe acoustic qualities that belong to the environment, such as reverberation, distance, muffling, or room tone.

## Reliability
Use concrete nouns, visible relationships, and chronological phrasing. Avoid contradictory states, excessive cuts, impossible transformations, ungrounded style stacking, and instructions that cannot be seen or heard.

common_guide.title: Profile Guide
common_guide.text:
## Observable multimodal writing
Write only camera-visible and microphone-audible facts. Establish visual style, composition, subject identity and count, wardrobe, prop ownership, environment, lighting, action, camera, dialogue, ambience, and sound. Do not infer hidden anatomy, off-frame content, prior action, unavailable audio, incidental reference attributes, or abstract meaning.

## Shots, timing, and Context Loop
Use `[Shot 1]` for the opening and keep only `[Shot 1]` while both camera presentation and principal action remain materially continuous. Add `[Shot N]` only when the camera materially changes or the principal action changes to a distinct observable beat. `[Shot 1]` has no timestamp. Every later shot begins on its own line as `[Shot N] At MM:SS.mmm, ...` with a realistic, strictly increasing start time inside the supplied duration; when duration is absent, use a 5.00-second timing window. For a same-camera action change, begin directly with the new observable action and result. Do not write `without a cut`, `the same continuous camera take continues`, or equivalent boilerplate. When camera, viewpoint, location, time, or edit materially changes, name the exact cut, transition, framing, or movement and the new information it reveals.

At every later shot, apply a concise Context Loop: re-anchor only the continuing identity and count, wardrobe and prop ownership, current body/object/contact state, screen position and direction, environment and lighting, camera framing and axis, and audible ambience needed to prevent drift. Do not repeat the full reference map. Give each shot one principal visible beat and a usable resulting state. A cut must reveal new subject, state, viewpoint, space, or time; use camera movement instead when only distance or angle changes.

## Camera language
Write camera motion naturally inside the shot. Use motion type—Zoom In/Out, Push In/Pull Out, Pan, Truck, Tilt, Pedestal, Arc Shot, Tracking Shot, Static Shot, POV, Roll, or motivated shake—with amplitude and speed only when meaningful. Pair movement with the visible result it reveals.

## Dialogue, visible text, and sound
Assign stable `(S1)`, `(S2)` speaker IDs in order of actual vocal events and reuse them. Put dialogue chronologically inside the applicable description field using exactly `<d>[Language] spoken text</d>`; keep speaker identity, delivery, and action outside `<d>`, with no quotation marks inside. Use native script when requested. For off-screen voiceover, say `says in an off-screen voiceover` and state that the on-screen character’s lips remain closed. Use `<scenetrans>` for speech crossing a cut and `<cutoff>` for speech truncated by the ending. Put exact visible on-screen text in double quotation marks.

Keep ambience, physical action sounds, and non-verbal human sounds in `overall_soundscape`; do not repeat dialogue there. Keep audience-only score in `non_diegetic_music`, describing instrumentation, tempo, rhythm, and dynamics; use `N/A` when absent. Diegetic music belongs in the timed description.

## Reference and dialogue syntax
Use Picture labels only for still-image evidence. Keep video-reference and audio-reference numbering independent, and never infer a missing modality. Bind a single subject as (S1); bind a coherent group as (S1,S2) when the same action applies to both. Dialogue must be verbatim in the requested language using exact <d>[Language] spoken text</d> tags, with speaker identity, delivery, and visible action outside the tag. Distinguish retained identity, object, motion, camera, and audio attributes according to the selected format rather than carrying an entire reference by default.

## Reference to Video canonical guide
Use the full-reference structure. Assign every referenced person, object, environment, picture, video, or audio a stable label, a narrow authority, and an explicit exclusion boundary. Keep label meanings stable across subject_definitions, summary, retention_analysis, detailed_description, overall_soundscape, and non_diegetic_music. path_guide.title: Generation Path Guide
path_guide.text:
## Full-reference six-field method
Use full-reference mode when references separately control identity, scene, style, action, motion, voice, audio, edit source, or reusable subjects. Output exactly `subject_definitions`, `summary`, `retention_analysis`, `detailed_description`, `overall_soundscape`, and `non_diegetic_music` in that order.

## Reference labels and authority
Use `<Subject N>` for reusable visible content; `<Picture N>` for concrete frame or storyboard anchors; `<Video N>` for editing, continuation, camera, cut, rhythm, or whole-video structure; and `<Audio N>` for copied or referenced audio. Keep every label’s meaning stable. Define one line per separately tracked item and state its bounded role. Do not define background context from the same single image as an extra subject unless it is separately controlled or environment-only.

## Summary and retention
Begin `summary` with the applicable task prefix assembled from `keyframe completion`, `reference generation`, `video editing`, `video continuation`, `audio reuse`, and `audio reference`, joined with ` + `. Summarize target and reference relationships without new labels. In `retention_analysis`, use one line per label and only the fixed visible markers `fully_preserved`, `partially_preserved`, `attribute_transfer`, `weak_reference`, or audio markers `fully_copy`, `partially_copy`, `reference`, `weak_reference`. List every actual shot where each reference applies.

## Detailed description
Write one or two style sentences before `[Shot 1]`, then a highly detailed playback-order description. At each actual shot establish composition, visible appearance and position, environment and lighting, action and state change, camera, current sound, and where each reference takes effect. Cite labels at first appearance and where their role applies. Keep `(Sx)` speaker IDs distinct from reference labels; bind referenced voices without inventing speech. Use the shared MiniMax timing, camera, dialogue, Context Loop, soundscape, and music rules.

common_guide.title: Profile Guide
common_guide.text:
## Observable and bounded prompting
Write only visible and audible direction. Preserve definitive user choices, stable subject count, identity, wardrobe, prop and voice ownership, scene, screen geography, action continuity, lighting, camera axis, dialogue, ambience, and sound. Do not expose analysis or commentary, and do not invent facts about unseen references.

## Shot construction and timing
Use `[SHOT 1]` while camera presentation and principal action remain materially continuous. Add `[SHOT N]` only for a material camera change or distinct principal-action beat. `[SHOT 1]` has no timestamp; later shots use `[SHOT N] At MM:SS.mmm, ...` with strictly increasing times inside the supplied duration or a 5.00-second fallback. For same-camera action changes, state the new action and visible result directly; never add `without a cut` boilerplate. Name real cuts, transitions, framing changes, or camera moves and what they reveal.

At each later shot, apply a concise Context Loop for continuing identity/count, wardrobe and prop ownership, body/object/contact state, screen direction, environment/lighting, camera framing/axis, and ambience. Give each shot one primary visible event and stable result. Pair every camera movement with what it reveals.

## Dialogue and finishing direction
Put exact spoken lines chronologically inside the applicable shot using `[Language] "spoken text"`; keep speaker, delivery, timing, and action in prose outside the quote. Use native script when requested. After the shot list, use only applicable finishing sections such as `[ACTING]`, `[LIGHT AND IMAGE]`, `[CAMERA]`, `[PRODUCTION SOUND]`, and `[NEGATIVES]`. Keep negatives short and observable—identity drift, swaps, broken geography, duplicate props, subtitles, unwanted music, or unmotivated edits.

## Reference labels and ownership
Keep image, video, and audio references in their own label families and numbering. Bind each source to a specific subject, object, environment, motion, camera, voice, or sound role. For grouped action, keep participant labels and ownership explicit. Write dialogue verbatim in the requested language and place delivery, speaker action, ambience, foley, and music in their designated bracketed sections.

In [REFERENCE USE], give each Picture, Video, or Audio token one bounded authority and state what incidental identity, pose, wardrobe, setting, camera, action, or sound it must not contribute. path_guide.text:
## Bounded reference authority
Start with `[REFERENCE USE]`. Map each available `<Picture N>`, `<Video N>`, and `<Audio N>` to one named production role and explicitly exclude incidental people, background, pose, framing, clothing, sound, or style. Keep upload order and token meaning stable; never rely on “respectively.” Images may define identity, wardrobe, objects, location, layout, materials, light, or style. Videos may define motion, performance timing, camera, edit rhythm, or serve as sole edit master. Audio may define timbre, accent, cadence, dialogue, music, or effects.

## Structured scene and control
Use only applicable `[IDENTITY / CONTINUITY LOCKS]`, `[SCENE]`, `[SCREEN GEOGRAPHY]`, `[SHOT LIST]`, `[ACTING]`, `[LIGHT AND IMAGE]`, `[CAMERA]`, `[PRODUCTION SOUND]`, and `[NEGATIVES]`. For performance transfer, preserve only named motion, timing, expression, or camera traits and reject source actors, clothing, location, and identity. For voice transfer, bind one audio reference to one named speaker, exact line, lip sync, and voice ownership. For editing, declare one `[SOURCE MASTER]`, exact `[EDIT]` targets, and a `[PRESERVE]` boundary for all untouched performance, occlusion, camera, timing, dialogue, and ambience.
